BASE CHANGE THEOREM BY A SMOOTH MORPHISM, AND APPLICATIONSby M. Artin
Contents

1. The base change theorem by a smooth morphism.
2. The specialization theorem for cohomology groups.
3. The relative cohomological purity theorem.
4. The comparison theorem for the cohomology of algebraic preschemes over \(\mathbb{C}\).
5. The finiteness theorem for algebraic preschemes in characteristic zero.

pages.title: 1. The base change theorem by a smooth morphism.

blocks.html: 1. The base change theorem by a smooth morphism.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 1.1

Let \(\mathbb{L} \subset \mathbb{P}\), \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), and

\[(*)\qquad \xymatrix{ X \ar[d]_{f} & X' \ar[l]_{g'} \ar[d]^{f'} \\ Y & Y' \ar[l]_{g} }\]

a cartesian diagram, with \(f\) quasi-compact and quasi-separated, and \(g\) universally locally \(0\)-acyclic (resp. univ. loc. \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\), resp. univ. loc. \(n\)-acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\)) (XV 1.11). Then for each sheaf \(F\) of sets (resp. of ind-\(\mathbb{L}\)-groups, resp. of abelian \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion) on \(X\), the base change morphism (XII 4.1.2)

\[\varphi^q : g^*(R^q f_*)F \longrightarrow (R^q f'_*)g'^* F\]

is bijective for \(q = 0\) (resp. \(q \leqslant 1\), resp. \(q \leqslant n\)).
In particular, applying XV 2.1, we obtain the

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.2

(Base change theorem by a smooth morphism). Suppose that the morphism \(g\) in (*) is smooth, that \(f\) is quasi-compact and quasi-separated, and that \(\mathbb{L} \subset \mathbb{P}\) is the complement of the set of residue characteristics of \(Y\). Then for each sheaf \(F\) of sets (resp. of ind-\(\mathbb{L}\)-groups, resp. of abelian \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion) on \(X\), the base change morphism \(\varphi^q\) above is bijective for \(q = 0\) (resp. for \(q = 0,1\), resp. for each \(q\)).

Proof of 1.1. We first treat the case where \(f : X \to Y\) is quasi-projective: it is nothing more than a combination of the base change theorem for a proper morphism XII 5.1 and definition XV 1.9. Indeed, we have a commutative diagram
\[\xymatrix{ X \ar[rr]^{i} \ar[dr]_{f} & & \overline{X} \ar[dl]^{\overline{f}} \\ & Y & }\]

where \(\overline{f}\) is projective, hence proper, and where \(i\) is an open immersion. Now we know (XII 5.1) that the base change theorem holds for \(\overline{f}\) whatever \(g : Y' \to Y\) may be. Since \(g \times_Y \overline{Y} : Y' \times_Y \overline{Y} \to \overline{Y}\) is again universally \(0\)-acyclic (resp. ...), we are immediately reduced, by (XII 4.4 (ii)), to proving the theorem for the morphism \(i\), that is, we are reduced to the case where \(f\) is an open immersion. Then the theorem is a consequence of definition XV 1.10 (ii).
We now treat the general case. The assertion is local on \(Y\), and so we may assume \(Y\) affine.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.3

We may moreover assume \(X\) affine.

Proof. Proceeding as in XII 6.1, we are reduced, in order to prove 1.1 for a given \(f\), to proving it in the situation deduced from the given one by base changes \(\widetilde{Y} \to Y\), \(\widetilde{Y}' \to Y'\), for a local morphism \(\widetilde{g} : \widetilde{Y}' \to \widetilde{Y}\) of strict localizations of \(Y',Y\) induced by \(g\), and to proving that the homomorphisms
\[(*)\qquad H^q(\widetilde{X},F) \longrightarrow H^q(\widetilde{X}',F') \qquad (\text{where } F' = g'^*(F))\]

are bijective for \(q \leqslant n\), where \(\widetilde{X} = X \times_Y \widetilde{Y}\), \(\widetilde{X}' = X' \times_{Y'} \widetilde{Y}'\). This therefore reduces us to the case where \(Y,Y',g\) are strictly local, and to proving in this case the bijectivity of the preceding maps, granting that 1.1 is proved for \(f\) affine. Now let \((X_i)\) be a finite covering of \(X\) by affine opens \(X_i\), and let \(Z\) be the sum scheme of the \(X_i\), which is therefore affine and equipped with a surjective morphism \(h : Z \to X\), whence a morphism \(h' : Z' \to X'\). Note that \(h\) is separated, and that it is affine when \(f\) is separated. This said, applying the descent lemma XII 6.8, we see that in order to prove the bijectivity of the maps (*) for \(q \leqslant n\) and for every \(F\), it suffices to prove the bijectivity of the corresponding maps \(H^q(Z,h^*(F)) \to H^q(Z',h'^*(F'))\), provided that the base change homomorphisms, for \(Z \to X\) and for the base change \(X' \to X\), are isomorphisms in dimension \(\leqslant n\). Now if \(f\) is separated, so that \(h\) is affine, this holds by hypothesis, which proves 1.1 when \(f\) is assumed separated. In the general case, we may then apply the preceding result to \(h\), which is always separated, and again conclude that 1.1 holds for \(f\), which proves 1.3.

Remark. One could also invoke the Leray spectral sequence for the open covering \((X_i)\) of \(X\), and its non-commutative variants, but this method, which is not essentially different from resorting to XII 6.8, has the disadvantage of forcing us to distinguish anew the three usual cases, work that has already been carried out in loc.cit.

To complete the proof of the theorem in the general case, it suffices to reduce the proof to the case where \(f : X \to Y\) is affine and of finite type, hence quasi-projective. By 1.3, we may assume \(X\) affine. Let then \(X = \varprojlim X_\alpha\), where \(f_\alpha : X_\alpha \to Y\) are affine schemes of finite type over \(Y\). We conclude with the usual passage-to-the-limit technique (VII 5).
Complements 1.4.

a) We leave it to the reader to verify that the same proof still yields a conclusion when one assumes that \(g\) is universally locally \((-1)\)-acyclic (XV 1.14): in this case, the base change homomorphism
\[\varphi^0 : g^*(f_*(F)) \longrightarrow f'_*(g'^*(F))\]

is injective for every sheaf \(F\) of sets on \(X\). On the other hand, assuming again \(n \geqslant 0\), one can supplement 1.1 by the following injectivity statement, likewise contained in the preceding proof: if \(g\) is universally locally \(0\)-acyclic, then for every sheaf of groups \(F\) on \(X\), the base change homomorphism \(\varphi^1\) of 1.1 is a monomorphism; if \(g\) is universally locally \(n\)-acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\), then the homomorphism \(\varphi^{n+1}\) of 1.1 is a monomorphism for every abelian \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion sheaf \(F\) on \(X\).

b) It is doubtless likewise possible to give an analogous injectivity conclusion starting from the hypothesis of local \(1\)-asphericity for \(\mathbb{L}\) of \(g\), by introducing the non-commutative \(2\)-cohomology invariants of GIRAUD's thesis, compare XII 5.11 (∗); the same question also arises for (1.6) and (2.3) below.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.5

Let \(K/k\) be a field extension, and let \(\mathbb{L} = \mathbb{P} - \{p\}\), where \(p = \operatorname{car} k\). Then \(\operatorname{Spec}(K) \to \operatorname{Spec}(k)\) is universally locally acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\) and universally locally \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\); if \(k\) and \(K\) are separably closed, then the preceding morphism is also universally acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\) and universally \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\).
Let us note at once the following consequence of (1.5):

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.6

Let \(K/k\) be an extension of separably closed fields, \(X\) a scheme, \(F\) a sheaf of sets (resp. of ind-\(\mathbb{L}\)-groups, resp. of abelian \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion groups) on \(X\), where \(\mathbb{L} = \mathbb{P} - \{p\}\), \(p = \operatorname{car} k\). Then the map

\[H^q(X,F) \longrightarrow H^q(X_K,F_K)\]

is bijective for \(q = 0\) (resp. for \(q \leqslant 1\), resp. for all \(q\)).

This indeed follows at once from the fact that \(\operatorname{Spec}(K) \to \operatorname{Spec}(k)\) is universally acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\) and universally \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\), and from the definitions.— Let us note that one can also interpret the preceding homomorphism on the \(H^q\) as being identified, by VIII 2.4, with the base change homomorphism
\[g^*(R^q f_*(F)) \longrightarrow R^q f'_*(g'^*(F)) \;,\]

where \(f : X \to \operatorname{Spec}(k)\), \(f' : X_K \to \operatorname{Spec}(K)\), \(g = \operatorname{Spec}(K) \to \operatorname{Spec}(k)\) and \(g' : X_K \to X\) are the obvious morphisms. Thus when \(X\) is quasi-compact and quasi-separated, the bijectivity of these homomorphisms can also be regarded, thanks to 1.1, as a consequence of the fact that \(\operatorname{Spec}(K) \to \operatorname{Spec}(k)\) is universally locally acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\) and universally locally \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\). This last fact therefore already implies 1.6 for \(X\) quasi-compact and quasi-separated, which manifestly suffices to entail that \(\operatorname{Spec}(K) \to \operatorname{Spec}(k)\) is universally acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\) and universally \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\) (XV 1.7, 1.6 (i)).

This therefore shows that to prove 1.5, it suffices to prove the first assertion of 1.5. Passing to the perfect closure of \(k\), which is licit by VIII 1.1, we may then assume \(k\) perfect. Every extension \(K\) of \(k\) is the inductive limit of its subalgebras \(A\) of finite type over \(k\), and, \(k\) being perfect, upon localizing such an \(A\), we may assume it smooth, so that \(K\) appears as a filtered inductive limit of smooth subalgebras. The latter being universally locally acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\) and universally locally \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\) by virtue of XV 2.1, we conclude thanks to XV 1.13 (ii), q.e.d.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 1.7

One should compare the invariance theorem 1.5 with XII 5.4, where one did not have to assume the torsion sheaf under consideration prime to the residue characteristics, but where on the other hand one must assume \(X\) proper over \(k\). Already in the case of \(H^1(X,\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})\), where \(X\) is an affine algebraic curve (for example the affine line) over an algebraically closed field \(k\) of char. \(p > 0\), the analogue of the preceding statements becomes false, because of the phenomena of "wild ramification" at infinity, implying that in such a case the classification of the principal étale coverings of group \(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}\) is essentially "continuous".

footnotes.html: (∗) This is indeed what is established in the book by J. GIRAUD.

blocks.html: 2. Specialization theorem for cohomology groups.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 2.1

Let \(\mathbb{L} \subset \mathbb{P}\), \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), and let \(f : X \to Y\) be a morphism of finite presentation that is proper (∗) and locally \(0\)-acyclic (resp. loc. \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\), resp. loc. \(n\)-acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\)). Let \(F\) be a sheaf of sets (resp. of ind-\(\mathbb{L}\)-groups, resp. of abelian \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion), constructible and locally constant on \(X\). Then the \(R^q f_* F\) are constructible and locally constant for \(q = 0\) (resp. for \(q = 0,1\), resp. for \(q \leqslant n\)), and for every geometric point \(\bar{y}\) of \(Y\), we have

\[(R^q f_* F)_{\bar{y}} \simeq H^q(X_{\bar{y}},F_{\bar{y}}) \;,\]

for these same values of \(q\).
Remark. Let us note that the last assertion is nothing but the base change theorem for a proper morphism XII 5.2.
Taking XV 2.1 into account, we immediately obtain the following corollary:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.2

(Specialization theorem for cohomology groups). Let \(f : X \to Y\) be a proper and smooth morphism, and \(\mathbb{L} \subset \mathbb{P}\) the complement of the set of residue characteristics of \(Y\). Let \(F\) be a sheaf of sets (resp. of ind-\(\mathbb{L}\)-groups, resp. of abelian \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion), constructible on \(X\). Then the \(R^q f_*(F)\) are constructible and locally constant for \(q = 0\) (resp. for \(q = 0,1\), resp. for all \(q\)), and for every geometric point \(\bar{y}\) of \(Y\), we have

\[R^q f_*(F)_{\bar{y}} \simeq H^q(X_{\bar{y}}, F_{\bar{y}})\]

for these same values of \(q\).
Remark. Taking \(n = 1\), and translating into terms of fundamental groups, we recover (SGA1 X 3.8) comparing the fundamental groups of the fibres of a proper and smooth morphism.

Proof of 2.1. Since we already know that the \(R^q f_*(F)\) are constructible XIV 1.1, it suffices, thanks to IX 2.11, to prove that for every specialization morphism \(\bar{y}_1 \to \bar{y}_0\) of geometric points of \(Y\), the corresponding specialization morphism (VIII 7.7)
\[(*)\qquad R^q f_*(F)_{\bar{y}_0} \longrightarrow R^q f_*(F)_{\bar{y}_1}\]

is bijective for the values of \(q\) under consideration. On this subject we have the following somewhat more general result (where it is unnecessary to assume \(f\) of finite presentation and \(F\) constructible):

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.3

Let \(\mathbb{L} \subset \mathbb{P}\), \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), \(f : X \to Y\) a proper morphism that is locally \(0\)-acyclic (resp. locally \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\), resp. locally \(n\)-acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\)), \(F\) a sheaf of sets (resp. of ind-\(\mathbb{L}\)-groups, resp. of abelian \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion) on \(X\), which is locally constant. Then for every specialization morphism \(\bar{y}_1 \to \bar{y}_0\) of geometric points of \(Y\), the corresponding specialization homomorphism \((*)\) above is bijective for \(q = 0\) (resp. for \(q = 0,1\), resp. for \(q \leqslant n\)). Moreover, in the case \(n = 0\), i.e. \(g\) locally \(0\)-acyclic, for every locally constant sheaf of groups \(F\) on \(X\), the homomorphism \(R^1 f_*(F)_{\bar{y}_0} \to R^1 f_*(F)_{\bar{y}_1}\) is injective; if \(n\) is arbitrary, for every locally constant abelian \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion sheaf \(F\) on \(X\), the specialization homomorphism \((*)\) is injective for \(q = n+1\).

There exists an integral strictly local scheme \(Y'\), and a morphism \(g : Y' \to Y\) sending the closed point \(y'_0\) to \(y_0\), the generic point to \(y'_1\): it suffices, for example, to take first the strict localization of \(Y\) relative to \(\bar{y}_0\), then its integral closed subscheme defined by a point above \(y_1\). Moreover, upon replacing \(Y'\) by its normalization in an algebraic closure of its function field, we may assume \(Y\) normal and \(k(y'_1)\) algebraically closed, so that \(y'_0\) and \(y'_1\) are geometric points of \(Y'\). Using the base change theorem (XII 5.1) for \((f,F,g)\), we are reduced, in order to prove 2.3, to doing so upon replacing \(Y, \bar{y}_0, \bar{y}_1\) by \(Y', y'_0, y'_1\), which reduces us to proving 2.3 in the case where \(Y\) is normal and strictly local, and where \(\bar{y}_0\) and \(\bar{y}_1\) are respectively its closed point \(y_0\) and its generic point \(y_1\). Moreover, using XII 4, we see that the specialization homomorphism \((*)\) then coincides with the homomorphism
\[H^q(X,F) \longrightarrow H^q(X_1,g_1^*(F)) \;,\]
where \(X_1 = X_{y_1}\) and where \(g : y_1 \to Y\) and \(g_1 : X_1 \to X\) are the canonical morphisms. Our assertion then follows from the following lemma (where \(f\) is no longer assumed proper):

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.4

With the preliminary notations of 2.3, let us drop the properness hypothesis on \(f\), assuming instead \(Y\) normal and integral, with generic point \(y_1\) such that \(k(y_1)\) is separably closed, and let \(X_1 = X_{y_1}\), \(g_1 : X_1 \to X\) the canonical morphism. Then the homomorphism

\[(**)\qquad H^q(X,F) \longrightarrow H^q(X_1,g_1^*(F))\]

is bijective for \(q = 0\) (resp. bijective for \(q = 0,1\), resp. bijective for \(q = n\), injective for \(q = n+1\)). Moreover, in the case \(n = 0\), i.e. \(g\) locally acyclic, for every sheaf of groups \(F\) on \(X\), the homomorphism (**) is injective for \(q = 1\).
An immediate argument (XV 1.6 (i) \(\Longrightarrow\) (ii)) shows that it suffices to prove the relation
\[F \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } g_{1*}g_1^*(F) \;,\]
and, for \(n \geqslant 1\), the additional relations
\[R^q g_{1*} g_1^*(F) = 0 \qquad \text{for } 1 \leqslant q \leqslant n \;.\]

Since these relations are local on \(X\) for the étale topology, and since \(F\) is locally constant for the étale topology, we may assume \(F\) constant, hence of the form \(G_X\), where \(G\) is a set (resp. an ind-\(\mathbb{L}\)-group, resp. an abelian \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion group). Let us note on the other hand that the hypothesis that \(Y\) is normal implies \(g_*(G_{y_1}) \xleftarrow{\ \sim\ } G_Y\) (IX 2.14.1), and the hypothesis that \(k(y_1)\) is separably closed implies that the \(R^q g_*(G_{y_1})\) vanish for \(q \geqslant 1\). On the other hand, the hypothesis that \(g\) is locally \(0\)-acyclic (resp. ...) implies that the formation of the \(R^q g_*(G_y)\) commutes with the base change \(f : X \to Y\) for \(q \leqslant n\), taking into account the fact that we may assume \(Y\) affine, and that then \(y_1\) appears as the projective limit of its affine open neighbourhoods, which are quasi-compact in \(Y\), so that we may apply definition XV 1.11 and the theory of passage to the limit VII 5. We thereby conclude that we indeed have
\[G_X \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } g_{1*}(G_{X_1}) \;, \qquad R^q g_{1*}(G_{X_1}) = 0 \text{ for } 1 \leqslant q \leqslant n \;,\]
which completes the proof of 2.4 and consequently of 2.1.
Remark. The preceding proof, via 2.4, simpler than our initial proof, is due to M. Lubkin.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.5

Under the conditions of 2.1, assume \(Y\) connected, and let \(q \leqslant n\). Then the \(H^q(X_{\bar{y}}, F)\), for the geometric points \(y\) of \(Y\), are all isomorphic to one another.

footnotes.html: (∗) For a less restrictive hypothesis than that of properness allowing one to obtain the same conclusions, cf. SGA 5 II 3 and SGA 1 XIII.

blocks.html: 3. The relative cohomological purity theorem.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3.1

Let \(S\) be a scheme. By a smooth \(S\)-pair \((Y,X)\) we mean an \(S\)-closed immersion \(i : Y \to X\) of smooth \(S\)-preschemes, that is, a commutative diagram of preschemes

\[\xymatrix{ Y \ar[rr]^{i} \ar[dr]_{h} & & X \ar[dl]^{f} \\ & S & }\]

such that \(f\) and \(h\) are smooth and \(i\) is a closed immersion. We denote by \(U = X - Y\), \(j : U \to X\) the open immersion, and \(g : U \to S\) the structural morphism. The codimension of \((Y,X)\) at a point \(y \in Y\) is defined to be the codimension at \(y\) of the fibre \(Y_s\) in \(X_s\), where \(s = h(y)\).
The codimension is therefore a locally constant function on \(Y\). We shall indicate by the phrase "\((Y,X)\) is of codimension \(c\)" that this function is even constant, with value \(c\).
Let \((Y,X)\) be a smooth \(S\)-pair and \(y \in Y\). Recall (SGA II 4.10) that there exist integers \(m\) and \(n\), a neighbourhood \(X'\) of \(y\) in \(X\), and an étale morphism
\[\phi : X' \longrightarrow \mathbb{E}^n_S = \operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{O}_S[t_1, \ldots, t_n]\]
such that \(Y' = Y \cap X'\) is the inverse image of the closed subscheme \(\mathbb{E}^m_S\) defined by the equations

One can express this result by saying that locally for the étale topology, each smooth \(S\)-pair \((Y,X)\) is isomorphic to the standard pair \((\mathbb{E}^m_S, \mathbb{E}^n_S)\) for suitable \(m\) and \(n\), where
\[\mathbb{E}^r_S = \operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{O}_S[t_1, \ldots, t_r] \;.\]

In the present section, we propose to compute the local cohomology sheaves \(\underline{H}^q_Y(X,F) = (R^q i^!)F\) (V 4 and VIII 6.6) for a smooth \(S\)-pair \((Y,X)\), with values in a locally constant abelian torsion sheaf \(F\) prime to the residue characteristics. We begin with some preliminary considerations:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.2

Let

\[\xymatrix{ U \ar[rr]^{j} \ar[dr]_{g} & & X \ar[dl]^{f} \\ & S & }\]

be a commutative diagram, where \(f\) is smooth, and \(j\) is an open immersion such that the fibre \(U_s\) is dense in \(X_s\) for each \(s \in S\). Let \(F\) be a sheaf of sets on \(S\). Then the canonical morphism

\[f^*F \longrightarrow j_* g^* F = j_* j^* f^* F\]

is bijective.

Proof. One easily reduces to the case where \(U\) is retrocompact in \(X\). Let \(\bar{s}\) be a geometric point of \(S\), \(\bar{x}\) a geometric point of \(X\) above \(S\), \(\widetilde{f} : \widetilde{X} \to \widetilde{S}\) the morphism of the strict localizations of \(S\), \(X\) at corresponding geometric points, and \(\widetilde{U} = U \times_X \widetilde{X}\). We have, with the obvious notations,
\[(f^*F)_{\bar{x}} = H^0(\widetilde{X},\widetilde{f}^*\widetilde{F}) \simeq H^0(\widetilde{S},\widetilde{F}) \;.\]
Consequently it suffices to prove that \(\widetilde{g} : \widetilde{U} \to \widetilde{S}\) is \(0\)-acyclic, which will imply
\[(j_* g^* F)_{\bar{x}} \simeq H^0(\widetilde{U},\widetilde{g}^*\widetilde{F}) \simeq H^0(\widetilde{S},\widetilde{F}) \;.\]

Since \(\widetilde{g}\) is a limit of smooth morphisms, it is locally \(0\)-acyclic (XV 2.1, 1.11), and by XV 1.12 it suffices to prove that the geometric fibres of \(\widetilde{U}/\widetilde{S}\) are \(0\)-acyclic, that is, connected and non-empty. Let \(\bar{s}'\) be a geometric point of \(\widetilde{S}\). Then the fibre \(\widetilde{X}_{\bar{s}'}\) is regular, connected and non-empty, and it follows from the hypothesis that \(\widetilde{U}_{\bar{s}'}\) is a dense open of \(\widetilde{X}_{\bar{s}'}\), hence connected and non-empty, whence the result.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.2.1

Under the conditions of 3.2, the functor \(X' \mapsto X'|U\) from the category of étale coverings of \(X\) to the category of étale coverings of \(U\) is fully faithful. In particular, for every finite group \(G\), the restriction map

\[H^1(X,G) \longrightarrow H^1(U,G)\]

is injective.
This follows from 3.2, via a standard argument which, for the convenience of references, we shall make explicit in a

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.2.2

Let \(f : X \to Y\) be a morphism of schemes, and let \(f^* : \operatorname{Et}(Y) \to \operatorname{Et}(X)\) be the inverse image functor \(Y' \mapsto Y' \times_Y X\) from the category \(\operatorname{Et}(Y)\) of étale coverings of \(Y\) to \(\operatorname{Et}(X)\). Equivalent conditions:

(i) \(f^*\) is faithful (resp. fully faithful).

(ii) For every étale covering \(Y'\) of \(Y\), denoting by \(f' : X' \to Y'\) the morphism deduced from \(f\) by the base change \(Y' \to Y\), the map \(U \mapsto f'^{-1}(U)\) from the set of subsets that are both open and closed of \(Y'\) to the set of subsets that are both open and closed of \(X'\) is injective (resp. bijective).

(ii bis) With the notations of (ii), for every constant sheaf of sets \(C\) on \(Y'\), the canonical map

\[H^0(Y',C) \longrightarrow H^0(X',f'^*C)\]

is injective (resp. bijective).

(iii) With the notations of (ii), the canonical map

\[\Gamma(Y'/Y) \longrightarrow \Gamma(X'/X)\]

is injective (resp. bijective).
The proof is left to the reader (cf. SGA 2, IX 3.1 and 3.2).

blocks.title: Remarks
blocks.html:
Remarks 3.2.3

One can considerably generalize 3.2, both in terms of sheaves of sets, by weakening the hypotheses on \(f\), and in terms of sheaves of groups with conclusions on the \(R^q g_*(f^*F)\) (cf. SGA 2 XIV and SGA 1 XIII). Analogous remark for 3.4 through 3.6.
"Let us recall" also the Zariski-Nagata purity theorem in its relative form:

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 3.3

(Relative purity theorem). Let

\[\xymatrix{ U \ar[rr]^{j} \ar[dr]_{g} & & X \ar[dl]^{f} \\ & S & }\]

be a commutative diagram where \(f\) is smooth, and where \(j\) is an open immersion such that for all \(s \in S\), \(X_s - U_s\) is everywhere of codimension \(\geqslant 2\) in \(X_s\). Then the functor \(X' \mapsto X'|U\) from the category of étale coverings of \(X\) to the category of étale coverings of \(U\) is an equivalence of categories.

Proof. That the functor is fully faithful was seen (3.2.1). The fact that it is essentially surjective will be deduced from the classical theorem. We are given an étale covering \(U'\) of \(U\); we must show that it extends to an étale covering \(X'\) of \(X\). Immediate easy reduction to the case where \(U\) is retrocompact in \(X\), then to the case where \(S\) is affine and of finite type over \(\operatorname{Spec} \mathbb{Z}\), \(X\) a connected scheme, and \(f\) of finite type.

We proceed by induction on \(n = \dim S\), the assertion being a consequence of the classical theorem (SGA 2 X 3.4) in the case \(n = 0\). Having uniqueness, we may apply the descent technique of SGA IX 4.7 to the normalization \(\overline{S} \to S\) in order to reduce to the case \(S\) (and hence \(X\)) normal (\(\overline{S} \to S\) being finite (EGA IV 7.8.3 (iii) (vi))). Moreover, upon enlarging \(U\), we may assume \(U\) maximal among the opens over which \(U'\) can be extended, and we must then prove \(U = X\). Otherwise, let \(x\) be a maximal point of \(X-U\), and \(s = f(x)\). Everything comes down to proving that we can extend \(U'\) over a neighbourhood of \(x\). We may assume that \(\dim \mathcal{O}_{S,s} = n \geqslant 1\) and that the theorem is already proved for dimension \(< n\). Set \(B = \mathcal{O}_{X,x}\), and let \(B'\) be the normalization of \(B\) in the ring of rational functions on the covering \(U'\) of \(U\); hence \(B'\) is a finite \(B\)-algebra (loc.cit.). It clearly suffices to prove that \(B'\) is an étale \(B\)-algebra.

Let \(A = \mathcal{O}_{S,s}\), \(0 \neq t \in \mathfrak{m}_A\), \(A_0 = A/tA\), \(B_0 = B/tB\). By the induction hypothesis, the restriction of the covering to \(U_0 = U \otimes_A A_0\) extends to an étale covering of \(\operatorname{Spec} B_0\); let us call it \(\operatorname{Spec} B_0^*\). Upon replacing \(X\) by a suitable étale covering of a neighbourhood of \(x\) (which is permissible), we may assume \(\operatorname{Spec} B_0^*\) completely decomposed over \(\operatorname{Spec} B_0\). We are thus reduced to the case where the \(B_0\)-algebra \(B_0'\) is completely decomposed outside the closed point of \(\operatorname{Spec} B_0\). Then the hypotheses of XV 3.3 are satisfied, whence the result.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.4

Same hypotheses as in 3.3. Then we have

\[(R^1 j_*)g^* F = 0\]

for each sheaf \(F\) of ind-finite groups on \(S\).

Reduction as usual to the case \(S\) noetherian, \(f\) of finite type, and \(F\) constructible. Let \(0 \to F \to G\) be an injection of sheaves of ind-finite groups on \(S\), and \(C = G/F\). It follows from 3.2 that the functor \(j_* g^*\) is exact, hence that \(j_* g^* G \to j_* g^* C\) is surjective, hence (XII 3.1) that \((R^1 j_*)g^* F \to (R^1 j_*)g^* G\) is injective. We may therefore replace \(F\) by \(G\), and we are thus reduced, by IX 2.14 and VIII 5.5, to the case where \(F = G\) is constant, with value an ordinary finite group \(G\). Let \(\bar{x}\) be a geometric point of \(X\), \(\widetilde{X}\) the strict localization of \(X\) at \(\bar{x}\), and \(\widetilde{U} = \widetilde{X} \times_X U\). Then it follows from 3.3 that we have
\[(R^1 j_* g^* F)_{\bar{x}} = H^1(\widetilde{U}, G_{\widetilde{U}}) \simeq H^1(\widetilde{X}, G_{\widetilde{X}}) \;,\]
and the latter is zero, whence the result.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.5

(Relative Abhyankar lemma). Let \((Y,X)\) be a smooth \(S\)-pair of codimension 1, such that \(Y\) is defined by an equation \(t = 0\) in \(X\). Let \(U = X-Y\) and \(V/U\) a principal Galois covering of order \(n\) prime to the residue characteristics of \(Y\). Set \(X' = \operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{O}_X[z]/(z^n-t)\), \(U' = U \times_X X'\), \(V' = V \times_X X'\). Then the covering \(V'\) extends uniquely to an étale covering of \(X'\).

Proof. Immediate reduction to the case \(S,X,Y\) affine and of finite type over \(\operatorname{Spec} \mathbb{Z}\). Uniqueness is a special case of 3.2.1. We shall deduce existence from XV 1.12: let \(\bar{s}\) be a geometric point of \(S\) and \(\bar{x}\) a geometric point of \(Y\) above \(\bar{s}\). Let \(\widetilde{f} : \widetilde{X} \to \widetilde{S}\) be the morphism of the corresponding strict localizations induced by \(f\), \(\widetilde{U} = U \times_X \widetilde{X}\), etc ... By descent, taking uniqueness into account, it clearly suffices to prove that \(\widetilde{V}'\) extends to an étale covering of \(\widetilde{X}'\), that is (since \(\widetilde{X}'\) admits no non-trivial covering) that \(\widetilde{V}'\) is a trivial covering of \(\widetilde{U}'\).

Let \(\widehat{U} = \varprojlim_m \widehat{U}_m = \operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{U}}[t^{1/m}]\), where \(m\) runs over the set of integers \(m\) prime to the residue characteristic of \(\widetilde{X}\). Then \(\widehat{U}/\widetilde{U}\) is an "infinite Galois covering" with abelian group \(G = \varprojlim_m \mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}\), and one sees immediately that it suffices to prove that \(\widehat{U}\) is \(1\)-aspherical for the set \(\mathbb{L} \subset \mathbb{P}\) complement of the residue characteristic of \(\widetilde{X}\).

Consider the morphism \(\widehat{f} : \widehat{U} \to \widetilde{S}\). It is a limit of smooth morphisms, hence locally \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\) (XV 2.1, 1.11 (ii)). By XV 1.12, it suffices to prove that the geometric fibres of \(\widehat{U}/\widetilde{S}\) are \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\). Let \(\bar{s}\) be a geometric point of \(\widetilde{S}\). The geometric fibre \(\widehat{U}_{\bar{s}}\) is the limit of the fibres \((\widehat{U}_m)_{\bar{s}}\). Consequently it suffices to prove that each principal Galois covering of some \((\widehat{U}_m)_{\bar{s}}\), of order prime to the res. char., induces a trivial covering of \(\widehat{U}_{\bar{s}}\). Replacing \(\widetilde{X}\) by \(\widetilde{X}_m = \operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{X}}[t^{1/m}]\) (which is again smooth over \(\widetilde{S}\)), we reduce to the case \(m = 1\), that is, \(\widehat{U}_m = \widetilde{U}\). Let \(V\) be such a covering of \(\widetilde{U}_{\bar{s}}\). Now \(\widetilde{X}_{\bar{s}} = Z\) is a regular strictly local scheme, and \(W = \widetilde{U}_{\bar{s}}\) is the open complement of a regular subset of codimension 1. We may therefore apply the Abhyankar lemma in its usual form (SGA1 X 3.6) to conclude that \(V\) induces a covering \(V_m\) on \(W_m\) which extends to an étale covering of \(Z_m\), for suitable \(m\). But \(Z\), hence \(Z_m\), being strictly local, it follows that this covering is trivial, hence \(V_m\) is a trivial covering of \(W_m\), q.e.d.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 3.5.1

When one does not assume the order \(n\) of \(G\) prime to the residue characteristics of \(X\), one can still prove the following: let \(m\) be the largest integer prime to the residue characteristics of \(Y\) that divides the order of \(G\), and suppose that for each point \(s \in S\), the covering \(V_s\) of \(U_s = X_s - Y_s\) has, at the maximal points of \(Y_s\), inertia groups of orders prime to the residue characteristics of \(Y\). Then the conclusion of 3.5 remains valid by taking \(X' = \operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{O}_X[z]/(z^m-t)\). One can also take for \(m\), more generally, any common multiple of the orders of the inertia groups just considered, assumed prime to the corresponding residue characteristics.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.6

(Cohomological purity in dimension 1). Let \((Y,X)\) be a smooth \(S\)-pair of codimension 1, and let \(F\) be a constructible and locally constant sheaf of groups on \(X\), of orders prime to the residue characteristics of \(X\). Then with the notations of 3.1, \((R^1 j_*)j^* F\) is locally isomorphic, as a sheaf of pointed sets, to \(i_*(F_Y/\operatorname{int}(F_Y))\), where \(F_Y = F|Y\) and where \(F_Y/\operatorname{int}(F_Y)\) denotes the quotient of \(F_Y\) by the operations of \(F_Y\) on itself by inner automorphisms.
Remark. The isomorphism of corollary 3.6 is not canonical.

Proof. One reduces immediately to the case \(X\) noetherian and connected. Since the assertion is local on \(X\) for the étale topology, we may assume that \(F\) is a constant sheaf, with value an ordinary finite group \(G\) of order \(m\) prime to the residue characteristics of \(X\), and moreover that \(\mu_{mX} \simeq (\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z})_X\). Let \(U = X - Y\) and \(U' = \operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{O}_U[t^{1/m}]\), which is an "essential" principal Galois covering of \(U\) with group \(\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}\) since \(\mu_{mX} \simeq (\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z})_X\). The principal coverings with group \(G\) of \(U\) that are trivialized over \(U'\) are classified locally on \(Y\) by \(H = \operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}, G) \bmod \operatorname{int}(G)\), which is a pointed set isomorphic to the underlying set of \(G/\operatorname{int}(G)\). We thus obtain a morphism from the constant sheaf \(H_Y\) on \(Y\) to \((R^1 j_*)G_U\), and it suffices to prove that it is bijective, which follows immediately from 3.5.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 3.7

(Cohomological purity). Let \((Y,X)\) be a smooth \(S\)-pair of codimension \(c > 0\). Let \(F\) be an abelian sheaf on \(X\) locally isomorphic (for the étale topology) to a sheaf of the form \(f^*(G)\), where \(G\) is a torsion sheaf on \(S\), prime to the residue characteristics (for example \(F\) a locally constant sheaf of finite groups of orders prime to the residue characteristics of \(X\)). Then, with the notations of 3.1, we have

\[\underline{H}^q_Y(X,F) = (R^q i^!)F = 0 \qquad \text{if } q \neq 2c \;,\]

i.e.

\[\begin{cases} F \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } j_* j^* F & \text{and} \\ (R^q j_*)j^* F = 0 & \text{if } q \neq 0 \;,\ 2c-1 \;, \end{cases}\]

and

\[\underline{H}^{2c}_Y(X,F) = i^*\big[(R^{2c-1} j_*)j^* F\big]\]

is a sheaf locally isomorphic to \(i^*(F)\).

Proof. The assertion is local on \(X\) for the étale topology; we may therefore (∗) assume \(F\) constant, hence if we wish \(F \simeq f^*(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})_S\) for the constant sheaf \((\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})_S\) on \(S\).

We first treat the case \(c = 1\). (The assertion for \((R^1 j_*)j^* F\), in the case \(F\) locally constant at least, would follow immediately from 3.6, but we shall deduce it anew.) Recall that \((Y,X)\) is locally isomorphic to the pair \((\mathbb{E}^{n-1}_S, \mathbb{E}^n_S)\), and if one replaces \(S\) by \(\mathbb{E}^{n-1}_S\), one reduces to the case where \(X = \mathbb{E}^1_S = \operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{O}_S[t]\) and where \(Y\) is the section \(t = 0\) of \(X/S\). The situation is locally isomorphic to the inclusion of the section at infinity in the projective space \(\mathbb{P}^1_S\). We may therefore take \(X = \mathbb{P}^1_S\), \(Y\) the section at infinity, and \(U = \mathbb{E}^1_S = X - Y\).
Let us examine the Leray spectral sequence
\[(R^p f_*)(R^q j_*)(\mathbb{Z}/n) \Longrightarrow (R^{p+q} g_*)(\mathbb{Z}/n) \;.\]

Now the abutment is zero for \(p+q > 0\), by XV 2.2. Moreover, the \(R^q j_*\) are concentrated on \(Y\) if \(q > 0\), which maps isomorphically onto \(S\) by \(f\), and on the other hand \(j_*(F|U) \xleftarrow{\ \sim\ } F\) by virtue of 3.2. It follows that \((R^p f_*)(R^q j_*) = 0\) if \(p\) and \(q > 0\), and that \(f_*(R^q j_*)\) determines the sheaf \((R^q j_*)\) if \(q > 0\), and finally \(R^p f_* j_*(F|U) = R^p f_*(F)\). The spectral sequence therefore reduces to isomorphisms
\[f_*(R^q j_*)(F|U) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } (R^{q+1} f_*)(F) \qquad \text{if } q > 0 \;.\]

But \((R^q f_*)(F)\) is computed fibre by fibre (XII 5.2), hence is zero if \(q \neq 0,2\), and is a sheaf locally isomorphic to \(G\) if \(q = 2\), as follows easily from XII 5.2 and IX 4.7. Hence \((R^q j_*)(F|U) = 0\) if \(q \neq 1\), and is a sheaf locally isomorphic to \(i^*(F)\) if \(q = 1\).

The case \(c > 1\) is now easily treated by induction: let \((Y,X)\) be a smooth \(S\)-pair of codimension \(c > 1\). It is clear that, locally on \(X\), one can find a subscheme \(Z\) of \(X\) of codimension 1 that contains \(Y\) and is smooth over \(S\), so that we have a commutative diagram
\[\xymatrix{ Y \ar[rr]^{u} \ar[dr]_{i} & & Z \ar[dl]^{v} \\ & X & } \;,\]
where each pair is a smooth \(S\)-pair (one should call \((Y,Z,X)\) a smooth \(S\)-triple), where the codimension of \((Z,X)\) is 1, and that of \((Y,Z)\) is \(c-1\).
Now we have the spectral sequence of composite functors
\[(R^p u^!)(R^q v^!)F \Longrightarrow (R^{p+q} i^!)F \;.\]

By the induction hypothesis, \((R^q v^!)F = 0\) if \(q \neq 2\) and is locally isomorphic to \(v^*(F)\) if \(q = 2\), whence again by the induction hypothesis, applied to \((R^q v^!)F\), that \((R^p u^!)(R^q v^!)F\) is zero if \((p,q) \neq (2c-2,2)\) and is locally isomorphic to \(u^* v^*(F)\) if \((p,q) = (2c-2,2)\), whence immediately the result for \((R^{p+q} i^!)F\), q.e.d.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.8

Let \((Y,X)\) be a smooth \(S\)-pair of codimension \(c\), \(n\) a natural integer prime to the residue characteristics of \(X\), and set

\[T_{Y/X} = \underline{H}^{2c}_Y(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}) \;,\]

which is a sheaf on \(Y\) locally isomorphic (for the étale topology) to the sheaf \((\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})_Y\) by virtue of (3.7). Let \(F\) be an abelian sheaf on \(X\), annihilated by \(n\), satisfying the condition stated in 3.7. Then we have (for the record) \(\underline{H}^i_Y(F) = 0\) for \(i \neq 2c\), and moreover we have a canonical isomorphism:

\[\underline{H}^{2c}_Y(F) \simeq i^*(F) \otimes T_{Y/X} \;.\]
Proof. One easily defines a canonical homomorphism
\[\varphi : i^*(F) \otimes T_{Y/X} \longrightarrow \underline{H}^{2c}_Y(F)\]
i.e. a homomorphism
\[i^*(F) \longrightarrow \underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(\underline{H}^{2c}_Y(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}), \underline{H}^{2c}_Y(F)) \;,\]

using the canonical homomorphism \(F \to \operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}, F)\). It remains to prove that \(\varphi\) is an isomorphism, which one verifies easily by following the proof given of 3.7.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.8.1

Under the conditions of 3.8, the formation of the \(\underline{H}^i_Y(F)\) commutes with any base change \(S' \to S\).
This is clear.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.9

(Absolute cohomological purity theorem). Let \(X\) be a regular scheme, \(Y\) a regular closed subprescheme of codimension \(c\) at each point. Suppose moreover that \(X\) is locally of finite type over a perfect field \(k\). Then, if \(n\) is prime to the residue characteristics of \(X\), we have

\[\underline{H}^i_Y(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}) = 0 \qquad \text{if } i \neq 2c \;,\]

and \(\underline{H}^{2c}_Y(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})\) is a sheaf on \(Y\) locally isomorphic (for the étale topology) to the constant sheaf \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\).
This is a special case of 3.7, taking into account that the hypothesis implies that \(X\) and \(Y\) are smooth over \(k\).

blocks.title: Remarks
blocks.html:
Remarks 3.10

a) In 3.8 one can make explicit the structure of the sheaf \(T_{Y/X}\); one finds that it is canonically isomorphic to the sheaf \((\mu_n)_Y^{\otimes c}\), where \(\mu_n\) denotes the sheaf of \(n\)-th roots of unity (locally isomorphic to the constant sheaf \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\)). The isomorphism in question is studied under the name of local fundamental class of \(Y\) in \(X\), in the somewhat more general situation of relative complete intersections, in Exp. XVIII devoted to duality.

b) It is very plausible that the conclusions of 3.9 and of 3.10 a) remain valid without postulating the existence of a base field \(k\), at least when \(X\) is an "excellent" prescheme. This is what will in any case be established in Exp. XIX when \(X\) is of characteristic zero, using Hironaka's resolution of singularities. As we shall see in SGA 5, one needs the "absolute purity theorem" (as well as resolution of singularities) notably in order to be able to establish the "local duality formula", (which is itself one of the major ingredients of the LEFSCHETZ-VERDIER formula).

footnotes.html: (∗) At least if \(F\) were assumed locally constant. The reader will convince himself that the proof which follows also applies, essentially, to the general case.

pages.title: 4. Comparison theorem for the cohomology of algebraic preschemes over \(\mathbb{C}\).

blocks.html: 4. Comparison theorem for the cohomology of algebraic preschemes over \(\mathbb{C}\).

Let \(X\) be an algebraic scheme over \(\operatorname{Spec} \mathbb{C}\). We shall compare the étale and classical sites on \(X\), and we take up again the notations of XI 4. The comparison theorem, which is the general form of XI 4.4, is the following:

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 4.1

Let \(f : X \to S\) be a morphism of finite type of schemes locally of finite type over \(\operatorname{Spec} \mathbb{C}\), so that we have a commutative diagram of morphisms of sites

\[\xymatrix{ X_{\text{ét}} \ar[d]_{f_{\text{ét}}} & X_{\text{cl}} \ar[l]_{\varepsilon} \ar[d]^{f_{\text{cl}}} \\ S_{\text{ét}} & S_{\text{cl}} \ar[l]_{\varepsilon} }\]

Let \(F\) be a sheaf of sets (resp. of ind-finite groups, resp. of abelian torsion) and suppose that we are in one of the following cases:

(i) \(f\) proper,

(ii) \(F\) constructible.

Then the base change morphisms XII 4.1.2 (∗)

\[\varphi : \varepsilon^*(R^q f_{\text{ét}*})F \longrightarrow (R^q f_{\text{cl}*})\varepsilon^* F\]

are bijective for \(q = 0\) (resp. for \(q = 0,1\), resp. for \(q \geqslant 0\)).
Let us note that the Grauert-Remmert theorem (XI 4.3 (iii)), which we had used in the proof of XI 4.4, is a special case of 4.1.

For the proof, we first treat the case \(f\) proper. In this case, the result will be a consequence of GAGA and of the base change theorem for a proper morphism, by an elementary argument that could have appeared in Exp. XIV. To treat the general case, we shall use in addition the resolution of singularities [1] and 3.7.
We may obviously assume \(Y\), hence also \(X\), of finite type over \(\mathbb{C}\).
Case \(f\) proper. We recall the following elementary facts:
(a) The topological space \(X_{\text{cl}}\) is locally compact.
(b) If \(f : X \to S\) is proper, then \(f_{\text{cl}} : X_{\text{cl}} \to S_{\text{cl}}\) is a proper map of topological spaces.
Indeed, (a) is trivial since locally \(X_{\text{cl}}\) is a closed set in some \(\mathbb{C}^n\). For (b) one reduces by Chow's lemma to the case where \(f\) is projective, this case being trivial.

Let \(F\) be a sheaf of sets (resp. ...) on \(X_{\text{ét}}\). For both morphisms \(f_{\text{ét}}\) and \(f_{\text{cl}}\), the formation of the \(R^q\) commutes with the formation of fibres (XII 5.2 and [2] 4.11.1). It therefore suffices to verify the theorem fibre by fibre, at the closed points of \(S_{\text{ét}}\).
In the following lemma, we do not assume that \(g\) is proper:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 4.2

Let

\[\xymatrix{ X \ar[dr]_{g} & & \overline{X} \ar[ll]_{h} \ar[dl]^{\overline{g}} \\ & S & }\]

be a commutative diagram with \(h\) proper, and let \(U\) be an open of \(X\) such that \(h\) induces an isomorphism from the open \(\overline{U} = U \times_X \overline{X}\) of \(\overline{X}\) onto \(U\). Let \(j : U \to X\) and \(\overline{j} : \overline{U} \to \overline{X}\) be the inclusions, \(F\) a sheaf of sets (resp. ...) on \(U\), and \(\overline{F}\) the sheaf induced on \(\overline{U}\). If theorem 4.1 is true for \((\overline{g}, \overline{j}_! \overline{F})\) it is also true for \((g, j_! F)\).

Proof. The theorem is true for \((h, \overline{j}_! \overline{F})\) because one is reduced to verifying it fibre by fibre, and one then has the two following cases: either the restriction of the sheaf to the fibre is zero, or the morphism \(h\) is an isomorphism. In these two cases, the result is trivial. One finds that
\[\varepsilon^* j_! F \simeq \varepsilon^* h_{\text{ét}*}(\overline{j}_! \overline{F}) \simeq h_{\text{cl}*} \varepsilon^*(\overline{j}_! \overline{F})\]
and
\[(R^q h_{\text{ét}*})\overline{j}_! \overline{F} = (R^q h_{\text{cl}*})\varepsilon^*(\overline{j}_! \overline{F}) = 0 \qquad \text{if } q > 0\]
for the values of \(q\) under consideration, hence that
\[(R^q g_{\text{ét}*})j_! F \simeq (R^q \overline{g}_{\text{ét}*})\overline{j}_! \overline{F}\]
and
\[(R^q g_{\text{cl}*})j_! F \simeq (R^q \overline{g}_{\text{cl}*})\overline{j}_! \overline{F} \;,\]
whence 4.2.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 4.3

To verify 4.1 for all data \((f,F)\) with \(f\) proper, it suffices to do so in the case where one assumes moreover that \(f\) is of relative dimension \(\leqslant 1\) and \(S = \operatorname{Spec} \mathbb{C}\) is a point.

Proof. Induction on the relative dimension. Suppose the result known in relative dimension \(< n\), and that \(n > 1\). As we have noted, we may carry out the verification fibre by fibre, that is, we may assume that \(S = \operatorname{Spec} \mathbb{C}\) is a point, and hence \(X\) of dimension \(\leqslant n\). Moreover, we may assume \(X\) reduced. Let \(\varphi\) be a rational function on \(X\) that is constant on no irreducible component of \(X\), \(U\) a dense open of \(X\) on which \(\varphi\) is defined, and \(\overline{X} \subset X \times \mathbb{P}^1\) the closure of the graph of the morphism \(\varphi : U \to \mathbb{E}^1\). We have a commutative diagram
\[\xymatrix{ & \overline{X} \ar[dl]_{h} \ar[dd]|{\overline{g}} \ar[dr]^{a} & \\ X \ar[dr]_{g} & & \mathbb{P}^1 \ar[dl]^{b} \\ & Y = \operatorname{Spec} \mathbb{C} & }\]

where the relative dimensions of \(a\) and \(b\) are \(< n\). By the induction hypothesis, the theorem is true for \((a,.)\) and \((b,.)\), whence we conclude that it is also true for \((\overline{g},.)\). Indeed, it is trivial for \(q = 0\); if \(F\) is abelian torsion on \(\overline{X}\), this follows from the morphism of Leray spectral sequences

\[\xymatrix{ \varepsilon^*(R^p b_{\text{ét}*})(R^q a_{\text{ét}*})F \ar@{=>}[r] \ar[d] & \varepsilon^*(R^{p+q} \overline{g}_{\text{ét}*})F \ar[d] \\ (R^p b_{\text{cl}*})(R^q a_{\text{cl}*})\varepsilon^* F \ar@{=>}[r] & (R^{p+q} \overline{g}_{\text{cl}*})\varepsilon^* F }\]

if finally \(F\) is a sheaf of ind-finite groups on \(\overline{X}\), let us note that since \(\varepsilon^*(R^1 \overline{g}_{\text{cl}*})\) is an effaceable functor, it suffices to prove (taking into account the result for \(q = 0\)) that \((R^1 \overline{g}_{\text{cl}*})\varepsilon^*\) is also effaceable (cf. XII 8.2), which follows from the exact sequence
\[0 \to (R^1 b_{\text{cl}*})a_{\text{cl}*} \varepsilon^* F \to (R^1 \overline{g}_{\text{cl}*})\varepsilon^* F \to b_{\text{cl}*}(R^1 a_{\text{cl}*})\varepsilon^* F \;,\]
and from the fact that \((R^1 b_{\text{cl}*})\varepsilon^*\) and \((R^1 a_{\text{cl}*})\varepsilon^*\) are effaceable thanks to the induction hypothesis.
Let now \(F\) be a sheaf of sets on \(X\). We have \(F \hookrightarrow h_{\text{ét}*}h^* F = G\). By the exact sequence
\[(4.3.1)\qquad F \to G \rightrightarrows G \amalg_F G \;,\]

we reduce (for \(q = 0\)) to proving 4.1 for \(G\), hence for a sheaf of the form \(h_{\text{ét}*}\overline{F}\). But for such a sheaf, the result will be a consequence of the theorem for \((\overline{g},.)\) and for \((h,.)\), and \(h\) is of relative dimension \(< n\), as one sees immediately.
Let \(F\) be an abelian torsion sheaf on \(X\). We have the exact sequence
\[(*)\qquad 0 \to j_! j^* F \to F \to i_* i^* F \to 0 \;.\]

Since \(U\) is dense in \(X\), we have \(\dim Y \leqslant n\), hence 4.1 is true for \((g|Y, i^* F)\), hence for \((g, i_* i^* F)\). It therefore suffices, thanks to the five lemma, to verify 4.1 for \((f,j_! j^* F)\), which follows from the theorem for \(\overline{g}\) (4.2).

Let \(F\) be a sheaf of ind-finite groups on \(X\). It suffices to prove that the functor \((R^1 g_{\text{cl}*})\varepsilon^*\) is effaceable for the sheaf \(F\), which follows from (*) and from the effaceability for \(j_! j^* F\) and for \(i_* i^* F\), i.e. from the theorem for \((g,j_! j^* F)\) (4.2) and for \((g,i_* i^* F)\) (induction hypothesis), q.e.d.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 4.4

To prove (4.1) in the case where \(f\) is proper, it suffices to prove the following: let \(X\) be a complete regular curve over \(\operatorname{Spec} \mathbb{C}\), and \(F\) a constant and constructible sheaf of sets (resp. ...) on \(X\). Then the morphisms

\[H^q(X_{\text{ét}},F) \longrightarrow H^q(X_{\text{cl}},F)\]

are bijective for the values of \(q\) under consideration.

Proof. Since it suffices to verify the theorem fibre by fibre, we are reduced by 4.3 to the case where \(X\) is proper and of dimension \(\leqslant 1\). The case of dimension 0 is moreover trivial, and it follows from this that the theorem is true for a finite morphism. Since \(f\) is proper, the cohomology of \(X_{\text{ét}}\) and of \(X_{\text{cl}}\) commutes with inductive limits (VII 3.3 and [2], 4.12.1), and we are therefore reduced to the case where \(F\) is constructible (IX 2.9 (iii)).

We apply IX 2.14. For a sheaf of sets, the exact sequence 4.3.1 and IX 2.14 show that we may take \(F = \pi_* C\), where \(\pi : X' \to X\) is finite, \(X'\) is normal, hence regular, and \(C\) is a constant sheaf on \(X'\). For a torsion abelian sheaf, we take a resolution of \(F\) by finite products of sheaves of the form \(\pi_* C\) and apply the spectral sequence of a resolution, and we again reduce to the case \(F = \pi_* C\). For a sheaf of ind-finite groups, we recall that it suffices to prove the effaceability of \((R^1 g_{\text{cl}*})\varepsilon^*\) for the sheaf \(F\), hence for a sheaf \(G\) into which \(F\) can be embedded, so we are again reduced to the case \(F = \pi_* C\). But it is clear by (VIII 5.5 and 5.8) that we may now replace \(X\) by \(X'\), whence the lemma.
To treat this last case, it evidently suffices (taking into account the cohomological dimension (IX 7.7 and [2] 4.14.1)) to prove that for a complete regular curve we have
(q = 0): \(X\) connected and non-empty \(\Longleftrightarrow X_{\text{cl}}\) connected and non-empty.
(q = 1): The base change morphism induces an equivalence between the category of étale coverings of \(X\) and the category of finite analytic étale coverings of \(X_{\text{cl}}\).
(q = 2): We have an isomorphism \(\varepsilon : H^2(X_{\text{ét}},\mu_n) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^2(X_{\text{cl}},\mu_n)\).

Now the first two assertions follow immediately from GAGA. For the last, note that we have \(H^2(X_{\text{ét}},\mathbb{G}_m) = 0\) (IX 4.5) and likewise, denoting by \(\mathcal{O}^*\) the sheaf of invertible holomorphic functions on \(X_{\text{cl}}\), \(H^2(X_{\text{cl}},\mathcal{O}^*) = 0\) (this follows from the exact sequence
\[0 \to \mathbb{Z} \to \mathcal{O} \xrightarrow{\ \exp\ } \mathcal{O}^* \to 0\]
and from the fact that \(H^2(X_{\text{cl}},\mathcal{O}) = H^2(X_{\text{ét}},\mathcal{O}_X) = 0\) by GAGA). Consequently the Kummer exact sequence IX 3.2 (resp. the exact sequence on \(X_{\text{cl}}\)
\[0 \to \mu_n \to \mathcal{O}^* \xrightarrow{\ n\ } \mathcal{O}^* \to 0 \;)\]
gives
\[H^1(X_{\text{ét}},\mathbb{G}_m)/n \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^2(X_{\text{ét}},\mu_n)\] \[(\text{resp. } H^1(X_{\text{cl}},\mathcal{O}^*)/n \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^2(X_{\text{cl}},\mu_n) \;) \;.\]
By GAGA, the canonical morphism
\[H^1(X_{\text{ét}},\mathbb{G}_m) = \operatorname{Pic} X \longrightarrow \operatorname{Pic} X_{\text{cl}} = H^1(X_{\text{cl}},\mathcal{O}^*)\]
is bijective, whence the result, which proves 4.1 in the case where \(f\) is proper.
Case \(F\) constructible. The proof is by induction on \(\dim X\). Suppose the result known when the dimension is \(< n\), and let us prove it when the dimension of \(X\) is \(\leqslant n\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 4.5

We may assume that \(f : X \to S\) is a dense open immersion and that \(F\) is constant.

Proof. As in the proof of 1.3, we may indeed assume \(X\) and \(S\) affine, hence \(f\) quasi-projective. Then we apply the reasoning of 4.4 to reduce to the case \(F = \pi_* C\), with \(\pi : X' \to X\) finite and \(C\) constant, whence, replacing \(X\) by \(X'\), to the case where \(F\) is constant. We may replace \(X\) by \(X_{\text{red}}\). Let
\[\xymatrix{ X \ar[rr]^{h} \ar[dr]_{f} & & \overline{X} \ar[dl]^{\overline{f}} \\ & S & }\]

be a commutative diagram such that \(\overline{X}\) is reduced, \(\overline{f}\) is projective, and \(h\) is a dense open immersion. It suffices to verify the theorem for the two morphisms \(h\), \(\overline{f}\) (cf. proof of 4.3), hence for \(h\) since \(\overline{f}\) is proper, hence for a dense open immersion.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 4.6

We may moreover assume \(S\) regular.
Proof. Let \(S' \xrightarrow{\ h\ } S\) be a "resolution of the singularities of \(S\)", i.e., a surjective, proper, and birational morphism such that \(S'\) is regular, and let
\[\xymatrix{ X' \ar[r]^{f'} \ar[d]_{h'} & S' \ar[d]^{h} \\ X \ar[r]_{f} & S }\]
be the cartesian diagram deduced from \(h\).

Let \(F\) be a constant sheaf of sets on \(X\). We have \(F \hookrightarrow G = h'_* h'^* F\) and deduce that it suffices (for \(q = 0\)) to verify 4.1 for \(G\) (cf. 4.3.1), that is, for a sheaf of the form \(h'_* F'\), where \(F'\) is constant on \(X'\). Now we have a commutative diagram (where we suppress the symbol "ét")

\[\xymatrix{ \varepsilon^* f_*(h'_* F') = \varepsilon^* h_* f'_* F' \ar[r]^-{a} \ar[d]_{d} & h_{\text{cl}*} \varepsilon^* f'_* F' \ar[d]^{b} \\ f_{\text{cl}*} \varepsilon^*(h'_* F') \ar[r]_-{c} & f_{\text{cl}*} h'_{\text{cl}*} \varepsilon^* F' = h_{\text{cl}*} f'_{\text{cl}*} \varepsilon^* F' }\]
and \(a\), \(c\) are bijective by the result for a proper morphism. To prove that \(d\) is bijective, it suffices to prove that \(b\) is, hence that
\[\varepsilon^* f'_* F' \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } f'_{\text{cl}*} \varepsilon^* F'\]
so we are reduced to the case \(S = S'\), hence \(S\) regular.
(Remark: We have used, without explicitly mentioning it, the finiteness theorem for a proper morphism XIV 1.1).

Let \(F\) be a constant torsion abelian sheaf on \(X\). It suffices to treat the case \(F = (\mathbb{Z}/n)_X\). Now the morphism \(h'\) induces an isomorphism over a dense open \(j : U \to X\) of \(X\); let \(j' : U' \to X'\) be the open \(h'^{-1}(U) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } U\), and \(Y = X-U\). We have \(\dim Y < n\) because \(U\) is dense, so the theorem is true for \((f,(\mathbb{Z}/n)_Y)\). By the exact sequence
\[0 \to j_!(\mathbb{Z}/n)_U \to (\mathbb{Z}/n)_X \to (\mathbb{Z}/n)_Y \to 0\]

and the five lemma, we reduce to proving the theorem for the sheaf \(j_!(\mathbb{Z}/n)_U\) and the morphism \(f\), hence by 4.2 to proving the theorem for \((hf', j'_!(\mathbb{Z}/n)_{U'})\). Now we have an exact sequence
\[0 \to j'_!(\mathbb{Z}/n)_{U'} \to (\mathbb{Z}/n)_{X'} \to (\mathbb{Z}/n)_{Y'} \to 0 \;,\]

and the theorem is true for \((hf', (\mathbb{Z}/n)_{Y'})\) by the induction hypothesis. It therefore suffices to prove the theorem for \((hf', (\mathbb{Z}/n)_{X'})\). But by the proper case, the theorem is true for \((h,.)\), and it follows, by the Leray spectral sequence for the pair of morphisms \(h\), \(f'\), that it suffices to prove it for \((f', \mathbb{Z}/n)\), whence the lemma in this case.

Finally, suppose that \(F\) is a constant sheaf of finite groups. Let us recall that it suffices to prove that the functor \((R^1 f_{\text{cl}*})\varepsilon^*(.)\) is effaceable for \(F\), hence for a \(G\) into which \(F\) can be embedded, hence for \(G = h'_* h'^* F\), that is, for a sheaf of the form \(h'_* F'\) where \(F'\) is constant on \(X'\). We have
\[\varepsilon^*(h'_* F') \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } h'_{\text{cl}*}(\varepsilon^* F')\]
and
\[0 \to (R^1 f_{\text{cl}*})h'_{\text{cl}*} \varepsilon^*(.) \to (R^1 f_{\text{cl}}h'_{\text{cl}*})\varepsilon^*(.) = (R^1 h_{\text{cl}}f'_{\text{cl}*})\varepsilon^*(.) \;,\]
so it suffices to prove the effaceability of this last functor for a constant sheaf. But we have the exact sequence
\[0 \to (R^1 h_{\text{cl}*})f'_{\text{cl}*} \varepsilon^*(.) \to (R^1 h_{\text{cl}}f'_{\text{cl}*})\varepsilon^*(.) \to h_{\text{cl}*}(R^1 f'_{\text{cl}*})\varepsilon^*(.) \;,\]

and the first term is effaceable, say effaced by the Godement resolution (XII 3.3), because \(h\) is proper. It therefore suffices to prove that the right-hand term is effaced by the Godement resolution, hence that \((R^1 f'_{\text{cl}*})\varepsilon^*(.)\) is, hence that the theorem is true for \((f', F')\) where \(F'\) is constant, whence the lemma.

End of the proof. We now assume that \(F\) is a constant sheaf and that \(f : X \to S\) is a dense open immersion, with \(S\) regular. The set-theoretic case now follows immediately from 3.2 and the analogous trivial lemma for the classical topology — indeed, we deduce that \(\varepsilon^* f_* F\) and \(f_{\text{cl}*} \varepsilon^* F\) are constant with the same value, hence isomorphic via \(\varphi\).

For \(q > 0\), we shall first reduce to the case where moreover \(X = S-Y\) with \(Y\) regular, i.e. to the case where \((Y,S)\) is a smooth \(\operatorname{Spec} \mathbb{C}\)-pair. Indeed, let us write \(X = S-C_1\), where \(C_1\) is equipped with the reduced induced structure, and define recursively
\[Y_\nu = \text{the dense open of regular points of } C_\nu \;,\] \[C_{\nu+1} = C_\nu - Y_\nu \;, \text{ with reduced induced structure.}\]
We have \(\dim C_{ u+1} < \dim C_ u\) because \(Y_ u\) is dense in \(C_ u\), whence a sequence
\[X = X_1 \subset X_2 = S-C_2 \subset X_3 = S-C_3 \subset \ldots \subset X_r = S \;,\]
where the inclusions \(i_ u : X_ u o X_{ u+1}\) are open immersions and where we have
\[X_ u = X_{ u+1} - Y_ u \;, \quad Y_ u ext{ closed in } X_{ u+1} \;, ext{ and regular.}\]

Now the direct image \(i_{ u*} F\) of a constant sheaf on \(X\) is constant (3.2), and the \(R^q i_{ u*} F\) are constructible and concentrated on subvarieties of \(Y\) of dimension \(\leqslant n-1\) (3.4, 3.6, 3.7) for the values of \(q\) under consideration. Hence by the induction hypothesis and the Leray spectral sequence (resp. the exact sequence XII 3.2), we reduce to the case of \(i_ u\), whence the announced reduction.

But for a smooth pair \((Y,S)\) we have explicitly computed the value of the \((R^q f_*)F\) for the étale topology (3.4, 3.6, 3.7), and an analogous and easy computation, which we leave to the reader, gives the analogous results for the classical topology. We deduce the theorem for \(f\) by a direct comparison.

footnotes.html: (∗) In fact, we use the base change homomorphism under more general conditions than those considered in Exp. XII, where we had restricted ourselves to a cartesian square of morphisms of preschemes. The reader will easily convince himself that the definition extends verbatim to an essentially commutative square of morphisms of sites. For further developments on this subject, see the following exposé.

pages.title: 5. The finiteness theorem for algebraic preschemes in characteristic zero.

blocks.html: 5. The finiteness theorem for algebraic preschemes in characteristic zero.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.1

Let \(k\) be a field of characteristic zero, and \(f : X \to S\) a morphism of finite type of schemes locally of finite type over \(k\). Let \(F\) be a constructible sheaf of sets (resp. of finite groups, resp. torsion abelian) on \(X\). Then the \(R^q f_* F\) are also constructible for \(q = 0\) (resp. for \(q = 0,1\), resp. for all \(q\)).

We make the hypothesis that \(k\) is of characteristic 0 because we shall make use of the theorem of resolution of singularities [1]. The proof is equally valid for characteristic \(p > 0\) if one admits resolution of singularities, provided that \(F\) is of orders prime to \(p\). We can thus deduce a result in characteristic \(\neq 0\) for \(\dim X \leqslant 2\), by applying the results of Abhyankar [3]. Another ingredient of the proof, besides the perennial base change theorem for a proper morphism, is the "absolute cohomological purity theorem" 3.9.

Let us recall that the theorem is already proved for a proper morphism and for arbitrary \(S\) (XIV 1.1). Moreover, in Exposé XIX (still in char. 0) we shall obtain the finiteness theorem under the much weaker hypotheses that \(S\) is an excellent scheme and that \(f\) is of finite type, by proving for such schemes the absolute purity theorem in the form indicated in 3.10.
In the case of characteristic \(\neq 0\) and a scheme of dimension \(\geqslant 3\), we have for the moment only the following easy consequence of XI 3.3:

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.2

Let \(X\) be a smooth algebraic scheme over \(\operatorname{Spec} k\), \(k\) a separably closed field, and let \(F\) be a sheaf of finite abelian groups (resp. of finite groups) which is locally constant, and of orders prime to the characteristic of \(k\). Then \(H^q(X,F)\) is a finite group (resp. a finite pointed set) for all \(q\) (resp. for \(q = 0,1\)).

Proof of 5.2. We may assume \(k\) algebraically closed (VIII 1.1). Induction on \(n = \dim X\). By XI 3.3 there exists a hypercovering of \(X\) by opens which are "good neighbourhoods". We reduce immediately, by the spectral sequence of a hypercovering, to the case where \(X\) is a good neighbourhood, hence admits an elementary fibration (XI 3.1)
\[\xymatrix{ X \ar[rr]^{j} \ar[dr]_{f} & & \overline{X} \ar[dl]^{\overline{f}} \\ & S & }\]

By (3.2, 3.6, 3.7), the sheaf \(j_* F\) is locally constant on \(\overline{X}\), \((R^1 j_*)F\) is locally constant on \(Y = \overline{X}-X\), and \((R^q j_*)F = 0\) if \(q > 0\). Consequently it follows from 2.1 that \((R^p \overline{f}_*)(R^q j_*)F\) is a locally constant sheaf on \(S\) for the values of \(q\) under consideration, and the result follows from the induction hypothesis and the Leray spectral sequence (resp. the exact sequence XII 3.2).

Proof of 5.1. The proof of 5.1 is very close to that of 4.1 for the case \(F\) constructible. We shall confine ourselves to indicating the main lines: Induction on \(\dim X = n\). We first reduce to the case \(X\) and \(S\) affine, hence \(f\) quasi-projective, by applying the method of the proof of 1.3. Next we apply IX 2.15 and (VIII 5.5 and 5.8) to reduce to the case where \(F\) is constant. We have a commutative diagram
\[\xymatrix{ X \ar[rr]^{h} \ar[dr]_{f} & & \overline{X} \ar[dl]^{\overline{f}} \\ & S & } \;,\]

where \(h\) is a dense open immersion and \(\overline{X}\) is proper, so the theorem is true for \(\overline{X}\) (XIV 1.1). It thus suffices to prove the theorem for \((h,F)\), that is, for a dense open immersion and a constant sheaf. Let \(h : S' \to S\) be a resolution of the singularities of \(S\) and
\[\xymatrix{ X \ar[d]_{f} & X' \ar[l]_{h'} \ar[d]^{f'} \\ S & S' \ar[l]_{h} }\]

the cartesian diagram deduced from \(h\). We reduce to proving the theorem for \(f'\), hence to the case where moreover \(S = S'\) is regular. By the induction method employed at the end of the proof of 4.1, we reduce to the case where \(Y = S-X\) is nonsingular, i.e. where \((Y,S)\) is a smooth pair, and we conclude by applying (3.2, 3.4, 3.6, 3.7).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.3

The proof of 5.1 just sketched is equally valid when one is given a left noetherian ring \(A\), annihilated by an integer \(n > 0\) (which must be assumed prime to the characteristic if the latter is not assumed to be zero, cf. remarks following 5.1), and when one considers constructible sheaves of left \(A\)-modules.

[2] GODEMENT, R. Théorie des Faisceaux, Paris, 1958.
[3] ABHYANKAR, S. Local uniformization on algebraic surfaces over ground fields of characteristic \(p \neq 0\), Ann. of Math., vol. 63 (1956), p. 491.
[4] SERRE, J.-P. Géométrie Algébrique et Géométrie Analytique, Annales Inst. Fourier 1956, p. 1-42 (Cited GAGA).
